Metric overview

Source: vignettes/articles/metrics-overview.Rmd
metrics-overview.Rmd

This package provides several ways to evaluate the performance of an embedding. They fall into four broad families.

Choosing a Starting Metric

User question Reasonable starting metric Decision supported by the result
Are the same nearby observations retained? nn_preservation() Whether local-neighborhood identity is preserved well enough for the intended use.
Do dense and sparse regions keep their relative local scale? local_radius_correlation() Whether scale distortion needs attention even when neighbor identities look acceptable.
Are broad distance orderings retained? random_triplet_accuracy() Whether the embedding preserves enough global ordering for the intended use.
Do known labels remain retrievable? roc_auc() or pr_auc() Whether same-label observations remain separated from other labels in the embedding.

Choose metrics to match the relationships an embedding should preserve. The table gives starting points.

Local Neighborhood Preservation

nbr_pres() compares neighborhoods from exact distance matrices. nn_preservation() and nbr_pres_knn() work with nearest-neighbor graphs and scale to larger datasets.

trustworthiness() and continuity() are also local-neighborhood metrics, but they use rank penalties rather than only counting shared neighbors. They are exact distance-matrix functions for small datasets. rnx_auc() summarizes rank-based neighborhood agreement over many neighborhood sizes; rnx_curve() retains the individual scales.

See the local preservation article for examples and related local diagnostics.

Local Scale Preservation

Neighbor identity does not say whether dense and sparse regions keep their relative scale. local_radius_correlation() compares the local radius around each observation in the input data and output embedding, using either the distance to the kth neighbor or the mean distance to the first k neighbors.

Local Graph Diagnostics

mutual_neighbor_correlation() compares the mutual-neighbor count pattern in the input and output nearest-neighbor graphs. It asks whether points with many or few reciprocal nearest-neighbor relationships in the input graph have similar counts in the output graph.

Global Distance Preservation

quadra also contains random triplet and random pair distance methods for global structure preservation:

  • random_triplet_accuracy() checks whether sampled distance orderings are preserved.
  • random_pair_distance_correlation() measures Pearson or Spearman correlation between sampled input and output distances.
  • random_pair_distance_emd() compares sampled distance distributions using Earth Mover’s Distance.
  • random_pair_distance_stress() compares matched sampled distances with a root mean squared difference.

For these metrics, Xin and metric_in define the reference geometry.

See the global preservation article for those metrics.

Input and Ordering Conventions

Sampled pair and triplet metrics require dense, finite inputs; graph metrics accept the sparse inputs supported by rnndescent.

nbr_pres() includes boundary ties, exact-rank metrics break ties by column order, and supplied-graph metrics use their stored order.

Euclidean and squared Euclidean induce the same ordering but different magnitudes. This distinction affects Pearson correlation, EMD, stress, and local-scale summaries, but not neighbor, triplet, or Spearman ordering.

Label Retrieval

roc_auc() and pr_auc() rank each observation’s neighbors by output distance and treat matching labels as relevant. They require the PRROC package.

See the label retrieval article for examples and return value details.
